description:
Team DU:NE is a team of six university students from Kyung Hee, Sogang, Gachon and Chung-Ang universitiy. We are taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Our team is now complete and we are not taking on any new members. Thank you to everyone who got in touch.

For any inquiries, please contact our team leader.

Team leader: Sanghyun Song
Email: ellfuge1507@khu.ac.kr
summary:
DU:NE helps people choose a landing site near the Moon’s south pole and understand why that site works. The project has two parts that link to each other.

The first part is a website - primarily for essential prior knowledge. The learning resources we curated explain why landing near the south pole is hard. The Sources page lists every dataset and paper we used. Checks page shows what we have tested and what we have not.

The second part is the mission portal. You pick a site and a landing date on a 3D Moon, and the portal shows where the Sun and Earth sit against the real horizon at that spot, hour by hour. From this, it works out when the solar panels get light and when the lander can talk to Earth directly.

Tools for this already exist, but they are hard to use and expect you to know the subject already. We built DU:NE so that mission planners, educators and learners can get an answer quickly and see why it is the answer. Every number in the portal comes from NASA data and is labelled with how far we have checked it. Where we have no data, the portal says so rather than guessing.
details:
What it does

DU:NE helps a mission planner choose where and when to land near the Moon’s south pole. You set the conditions a mission needs, such as minimum sunlight and Earth visibility. The portal then ranks 25,992 grid cells between 75°S and the pole on a 5 km grid. You can also click a site on a 3D Moon and explore it directly.

Planning at the pole is hard because the Sun stays low in the sky. A ridge can hide it for long periods or block the line of sight to Earth. Where terrain data is available, DU:NE builds the local horizon from LOLA elevation data and takes Sun and Earth positions from SPICE ephemeris tables. It labels approximate models used where terrain data or table coverage is unavailable.


No prior knowledge is needed to get started. The homepage explains the basics of lunar landing planning and how to use the navigator. Users can explore the learning resources, data sources and validation notes before building a plan in the mission portal.

How a plan is built

The Plan tab has nine steps. Each one uses the values set in the steps before it.

  1. Mission setup. Pick a profile (long-term base, landing reconnaissance, water prospecting, or your own weights) and set requirements such as minimum sunlight and Earth visibility. Set the lander’s mass, thrust, power source, battery and power use. Places that fail the conditions are faded out of the map.
  2. Pick site and date. Choose a site from the map, ranking, list or coordinates, then set one landing time or a search period. Compare site and date pairs and check when sunlight and Earth visibility overlap. For catalog sites with local terrain data, you can also check how much of a chosen landing-error radius meets the slope limit and how much has measured terrain coverage.
  3. Base layout. Place the landing pad, power, water mining and habitat around the site and check the distances between them. The portal warns when the landing site is near an observed lobate scarp. You can turn off base layout for missions that do not need a base.
  4. Mission analysis. A simulation follows battery, Earth visibility and estimated data sent from landing to the end of the mission. It checks the surface operations targets and explains any stop. You can also estimate panel and battery sizes, find panel locations, check ground-station contact windows and simulate up to a year of solar-powered base operations.
  5. Orbit analysis. Using the chosen site, landing time and lander settings, the browser computes a path from a near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) through low lunar orbit to touchdown. It uses NASA ephemeris, GRAIL gravity, LOLA terrain and finite-duration burns to check fuel use, landing error and descent and contact limits. It shows the computed path in 3D, or explains why it could not find a path that meets the checks and suggests adjustments. Current coverage is 75–90°S, with landing dates from November 2026 through January 2027 (UTC).
  6. Replanning. If the planned landing is delayed by 3, 7, 14 or 30 days, the portal rechecks surface conditions and offers the same site on another date, or another site on the same date. It compares sunlight, earth visibility and darkness across the alternatives. The revised orbit is calculated separately in Orbit analysis.
  7. Compare. Compare up to four site and date choices side by side, and two saved sets of conditions (A and B) to see how much their top candidates overlap. You can also find places with similar sunlight and Earth-visibility patterns and explore the balance between access to permanently shadowed regions and power and communication conditions.
  8. Past missions. The portal replays the sky for 16 past landings, from Apollo 11 to IM-2 Athena, and lists missions with conditions like your plan, along with their outcomes. It can also find dates at your site with the same time since sunrise as a past landing and add them to the comparison.
  9. Validation. Compare the portal’s calculations with NASA data and see the differences and limitations. You can also inspect the current mission’s orbit inputs, checks and warnings. Passing means the plan meets the implemented model’s checks; it does not guarantee real mission safety.

Mission settings can be saved and loaded again, and results can be exported as reports and CSV files. Candidate rankings use surface conditions. Orbit results are attached only to calculations with matching inputs, and candidates without an orbit calculation are marked separately.

How we checked it

The latest recorded ephemeris checks compare Sun and Earth directions with JPL Horizons reference data at selected locations and times. The largest angular difference was about 0.00061° within those test cases.

An earlier comparison of long-term sunlight across the 25,992 cells gave a correlation of 0.90 and an RMSE of about 6 percentage points against the PGDA69 maps. A comparison with LROC wide-angle camera illumination at 88–90°S gave similar results. The periods, observer heights and resolutions differ, and the inputs used at the time are not fully traceable. We therefore keep these as historical reference results, separate from checks that have been rerun.

We also kept comparisons that do not agree well. Sun visibility at different mast heights differed from the JPL reference by about 37 percentage points RMSE, and the coordinate-axis interpretation of the reference point is still unconfirmed. A comparison of longest continuous sunlight across 130 candidate points over several years gave a rank correlation of 0.46. It used an assumed midsummer period because the source did not define one.

Earth visibility does not guarantee a working radio link. Contact windows are estimated from terrain and ground-station visibility, and data volume uses the selected transmission rate. Likewise, the share of a landing-error radius that meets a slope limit is not a landing success probability.

Tools and structure

DU:NE is a TypeScript web app that runs in the browser, with the 3D Moon and trajectories drawn in WebGL. Cloudflare Workers serve the static files. A Python pipeline prepares the NASA data, while surface analysis and orbit calculations run in the browser. Heavy calculations use Web Workers, so no separate calculation server or database is needed.

The code is checked with unit tests and browser integration tests. The homepage stores the learning resources, sources and validation guides, so the mission portal can stay focused on planning and analysis.

All NASA data and other sources are listed in the fields below.

PGDA 69: south pole average illumination, Earth visibility and permanent shadow

LROC WAC south pole illumination percentage
LROC NAC south pole permanent shadow polygons

NASA Visible Earth: Blue Marble (Earth texture)
NAIF generic SPICE kernels (de440s, lunar orientation, leap seconds)
DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook 810-005, module 301 (antenna coordinates and horizon masks)
PDS CLPS retroreflector location, IM-1 Odysseus
PDS CLPS retroreflector location, IM-2 Athena
